report:
Based on my research, the evidence does **not** clearly support "yes" — the honest answer is "uncertain/inconclusive," not a confident yes.

**What the strongest evidence shows:**

The most authoritative source is the Cochrane systematic review (Barnes et al., updated 2019), which pooled randomized controlled trials comparing hypnotherapy to no treatment or other cessation methods (nicotine replacement therapy, counseling, etc.). Its conclusion: evidence is **insufficient** to determine whether hypnotherapy is more effective than other treatments or than no treatment at all, largely because included trials were small, heterogeneous, and at high risk of bias (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD004407.pub4/full).

A 2021 Cochrane umbrella review of smoking cessation interventions reaffirmed this "uncertain effect" conclusion for hypnosis specifically (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1330362/full).

**On the other side:** Some individual trials report positive results — for example, one RCT found hypnotherapy outperformed nicotine replacement therapy alone, and a broader 2025 review (Ekanayake & Elkins) of 63 studies since 1968 reported generally positive support for hypnosis (https://www.ishhypnosis.org/encyclopedia/the-potential-benefit-of-hypnosis-for-smoking-cessation/). However, these studies are often smaller, less rigorously controlled, or funded/conducted by hypnosis practitioners, which the Cochrane reviewers flag as limiting confidence.

**Bottom line:** The highest-quality, most rigorous evidence (Cochrane) says we cannot yet confidently conclude hypnosis works better than other methods or placebo — it's "possibly helpful but unproven," not a clear "yes." Individual positive trials exist, but methodological weaknesses prevent a firm conclusion. I'd revise your view from "yes" to "the evidence is currently inconclusive, with some promising but not definitive studies."
